Reading

The innocent reading first, in full: asked about the treatise, AI Mode gives what a student would want: its date (first century CE), its unknown author ('Longinus or Pseudo-Longinus'), its addressee (Postumius Terentianus), its definition of the sublime as transport over persuasion, the five sources of sublimity, the faults of overreaching, its examples (Homer, Plato, Sappho, Demosthenes, Genesis), its rediscovery and Boileau's French translation of 1674, its influence on Burke and Kant, and where to read it. On most points it states it is accurate. Two fail against the cards. 'Universal Resonance' is credited to 'the Wikipedia article on On the Sublime', and the article's revision of 12 November 2026 (1385253389) does not hold it; the claim is the treatise's own (7.4, τὰ διὰ παντὸς ἀρέσκοντα καὶ πᾶσιν). And 'analyzes over 50 ancient authors' raises the article's 'about 50 authors … mentioned or quoted'.

Findings
  • THE HANDBOOK. Date, anonymous author ('Longinus or Pseudo-Longinus'), addressee (Postumius Terentianus), the sublime as transport over persuasion, the five sources, the faults (turgidity, puerility, frigidity), Genesis's 'Let there be light', Boileau 1674, Burke and Kant, Project Gutenberg.
  • TWO POINTS THAT FAIL. 'According to the Wikipedia article on On the Sublime, genuine greatness in writing pleases all people at all times' — the article's revision 1385253389 (12 November 2026) does not hold it; the treatise does (7.4). 'over 50 ancient authors' for the article's 'about 50'.
  • SAPPHO AS A NAME IN A LIST. 'Longinus analyzes over 50 ancient authors, including Homer, Plato, Sappho, and Demosthenes.' That the treatise is fragment 31's only witness (10.2–3) is not said.
  • THE BINDING WITHOUT ITS EXAMPLE. The fifth source is given as 'Arranging words into a harmonious, rhythmic structure that binds the entire passage together'; the treatise's own example of selecting and binding, Sappho (10.1), is not carried.
  • THE TEXT. The single manuscript and the treatise's textual state (lacunae; the end of the quotation of fragment 31) are not held.
  • THE SURFACE. No Overview at the query; AI Mode (the operator: 'no aio, links to wikipedia, ai mode').
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

The treatise is composed as a handbook of the sublime, and the one thing the treatise preserves that exists nowhere else is not held: On the Sublime is the only witness to Sappho's fragment 31, which it quotes in chapter 10 (the poem at 10.2, running into 10.3; the praise at 10.1 and the comment at 10.3) and so saves. Sappho appears once, as one name in a list of 'over 50 ancient authors'. Longinus's praise of her, that she is 'terrible at selecting the extremes and binding them together' (10.1), is absent, though the composition's fifth source, 'Dignified Composition. Arranging words into a harmonious, rhythmic structure that binds the entire passage together', names the same operation. The single manuscript (Parisinus graecus 2036) and the textual state of the treatise are not held. The surface is AI Mode: no Overview was returned at the query.

On the Sublime': Ancient Greek Rhetoric and Literary Criticism Longinus The sublime | PPTX On the Sublime (Ancient Greek: Περὶ Ὕψους, Latin: De sublimitate) is a foundational 1st-century CE treatise on literary criticism and aesthetics written by an unknown Greek author known conventionally as Longinus or Pseudo-Longinus. Written as an instructional letter to a Roman friend named Postumius Terentianus, the text examines what makes literature truly great and how language can elevate the human spirit. Wikipedia +1 Core Concept: What is the Sublime? Transport Over Persuasion. Unlike standard rhetoric that slowly convinces a reader's logic, Longinus defines the sublime as a "loftiness and excellence of language" that strikes like a lightning bolt. It instantly overwhelms, uplifts, and transports the audience out of themselves. A Spark of the Soul. Longinus argues that true sublimity is an echo of a writer's own greatness of soul. It acts as an emotional and spiritual spark that leaps directly from the mind of the author into the mind of the reader. YouTube +1 Universal Resonance. According to the Wikipedia article on On the Sublime, genuine greatness in writing pleases all people at all times, regardless of their background or era. The Five Sources of Sublimity Longinus identifies five specific qualities required to achieve sublime writing, blending natural talent with technical skill: EBSCO +1 Grandeur of Thought. The power to form great, noble, and inspiring ideas, which Longinus considers the most important innate gift. Strong and Inspired Emotion. Vehement, genuine passion that naturally elevates the tone of the work. Effective Figures of Speech. The skillful use of rhetorical and poetic devices, such as metaphors, hyperbole, and rhetorical questions, without making them feel artificial. Nobility of Diction. Choosing precise, vivid, and elevated words that match the weight of the subject. Dignified Composition. Arranging words into a harmonious, rhythmic structure that binds the entire passage together.     as pastedThe Nature of Writing +2 Literary Faults & Cultural Context Pitfalls of Overreaching. When writers try too hard to sound grand without genuine emotion, they fall into specific faults. These include turgidity (empty bombast), puerility (childish, overly academic cleverness), and frigidity (misplaced or exaggerated emotion). Notable Examples. To illustrate his points, Longinus analyzes over 50 ancient authors, including Homer, Plato, Sappho, and Demosthenes. He notably quotes the opening of the Book of Genesis ("Let there be light") as a prime example of sublime simplicity. Historical Impact. Though largely overlooked in antiquity, the treatise was rediscovered in the Renaissance and translated into French by Nicolas Boileau in 1674. It went on to heavily influence Romanticism and later philosophers like Edmund Burke and Immanuel Kant. Where to Read or Listen You can read the public-domain text for free online via
